config.title: Memory Leak Hunt

intro.title: Memory Leak Hunt
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular application that demonstrates how memory leaks can occur and how to prevent them. You will learn the core concept of unsubscribing from Observables to release resources when a component is destroyed. The main technologies involved are Angular components, RxJS Observables, and lifecycle hooks like ngOnDestroy. By the end, you'll understand why memory leaks happen and how to write cleaner, more efficient Angular code.
intro.usecase: Memory leaks in Angular applications commonly occur in long-running, interactive UIs like real-time dashboards, data tables with filters, and complex single-page applications. For example, a financial dashboard that continuously streams live market data can accumulate orphaned subscriptions and event listeners if components are not properly cleaned up when navigating between views. Developers must actively hunt for these leaks to prevent gradual performance degradation and browser crashes, especially in applications with dynamic content loading, modal dialboards, or real-time chat interfaces where components are frequently created and destroyed.

objectives: Implement ngOnDestroy lifecycle hook to clean up subscriptions
Apply the async pipe in templates to automatically manage observables
Construct a service that properly unsubscribes from event emitters
Configure takeUntil operator to control observable completion
Initialize component properties with null to prevent memory retention
Manipulate DOM event listeners using Renderer2 for proper cleanup
Integrate OnDestroy interface to enforce cleanup patterns
Update component state to release references when components are destroyed

steps.instruction: Create the MemoryLeakHuntComponent class with the @Component decorator, including selector and template metadata.
steps.hint: Use the imported Component decorator and define a class that implements OnInit and OnDestroy.

steps.title: Implement OnInit interface and define ngOnInit method
steps.instruction: In the MemoryLeakHuntComponent class, implement the OnInit interface and define an empty ngOnInit method.
steps.hint: Add 'implements OnInit' after the class name and create a public ngOnInit() method that returns void.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will implement the OnInit interface and have an empty ngOnInit method ready for initialization logic.
successCriteria: MemoryLeakHuntComponent implements OnInit and has a public ngOnInit method that returns void.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've both implemented the OnInit interface (using 'implements OnInit') and defined the ngOnInit method with the correct signature (public, returns void).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't yet implement OnInit or have the ngOnInit method. Remember to add 'implements OnInit' after the class name and create a public ngOnInit(): void method.

steps.title: Implement OnDestroy interface and define ngOnDestroy method
steps.instruction: In your MemoryLeakHuntComponent class, implement the OnDestroy interface and create an empty ngOnDestroy method.
steps.hint: Add 'OnDestroy' to the class's 'implements' list and define a method named 'ngOnDestroy' with no return type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now implements both OnInit and OnDestroy interfaces, with empty lifecycle methods defined.
successCriteria: OnDestroy is added to the 'implements' list and an empty ngOnDestroy method is defined in the class.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added 'OnDestroy' to the 'implements' list and created a method named 'ngOnDestroy' with no parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should implement both OnInit and OnDestroy interfaces. Add 'OnDestroy' to the 'implements' list and define an empty 'ngOnDestroy' method.

steps.title: Add component state properties for timer and data
steps.instruction: Inside the MemoryLeakHuntComponent class, add two properties: a timer property of type number and a data property of type any[].
steps.hint: Declare these properties directly in the class body, above the ngOnInit method. Use TypeScript type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have timer and data properties declared, ready to be used for demonstrating potential memory leaks.
successCriteria: The MemoryLeakHuntComponent class contains a timer property of type number and a data property of type any[].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added one property, but need both timer (number) and data (any[]).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class doesn't have both required properties. Add timer: number and data: any[] inside the class.

steps.title: Create a simulated data stream in ngOnInit
steps.instruction: Inside the ngOnInit method, create an interval observable using RxJS's interval function that emits every second and updates the data property with the current count.
steps.hint: Use RxJS's interval function to create an observable that emits sequential numbers every 1000 milliseconds. Subscribe to it and update the data property with the emitted value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ngOnInit method will now contain an interval observable that updates the data property every second, simulating a data stream that needs cleanup.
successCriteria: An interval observable is created in ngOnInit that emits every 1000ms and updates the data property with the emitted value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using RxJS's interval function and subscribing to update the data property. Check that the interval emits every 1000ms.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interval observable wasn't properly created. Remember to import interval from 'rxjs', create an observable that emits every 1000ms, and subscribe to update the data property.

steps.title: Subscribe to the data stream and store the subscription
steps.instruction: Inside the ngOnInit method, subscribe to the interval observable and assign the returned subscription to the dataSubscription property.
steps.hint: Call the subscribe method on the interval observable and assign the result to this.dataSubscription.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: subscribing to an observable
const subscription = interval(1000).subscribe(value => console.log(value));
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now subscribes to the interval observable and stores the subscription reference for proper cleanup.
successCriteria: The interval observable is subscribed to and the subscription is assigned to the dataSubscription property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're assigning the subscription to the dataSubscription property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The subscription wasn't properly stored. Remember to call subscribe() on the interval observable and assign the result to this.dataSubscription.

steps.title: Add cleanup logic in ngOnDestroy
steps.instruction: Inside the ngOnDestroy method, add logic to unsubscribe from the dataSubscription if it exists.
steps.hint: Check if the subscription property is defined before calling unsubscribe() on it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ngOnDestroy method now includes proper cleanup logic to prevent memory leaks by unsubscribing from the observable subscription.
successCriteria: ngOnDestroy contains an if statement that checks if dataSubscription exists and calls unsubscribe() on it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if the subscription exists before calling unsubscribe().
steps.feedbackWrong: The cleanup logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to check if dataSubscription exists and call unsubscribe() on it.

steps.title: Add a button to manually trigger cleanup
steps.instruction: Add a button element to your component's template with a click handler that calls the ngOnDestroy method to manually test cleanup functionality.

<button (click)="ngOnDestroy()">Clean Up</button>

successCriteria: A button element with (click)="ngOnDestroy()" is added to the component's template.
